title: AGI and Beyond
tagline: The most consequential argument nobody has settled.
description: Definitions, scaling debates, alignment, forecasting, and economic transformation — taught as live disagreements, not settled facts. You pass a checkpoint here by understanding the argument's structure, not by picking the 'right' side.

concepts.title: What would even count as AGI
concepts.summary: There is no agreed definition — and the definition you pick largely determines your timeline.

cards.h: Three definitions that don't agree
cards.md:
'Artificial general intelligence' hides at least three different claims:

- **Cognitive breadth:** a system matching humans across the full range of cognitive tasks — reasoning, learning new domains, transfer.
- **Economic replacement:** a system that can do most economically valuable work at or above human cost-quality (a definition OpenAI's charter made famous).
- **Autonomy:** a system that can pursue long-horizon goals in the world with human-level reliability, not just answer questions.

These come apart in practice. A model can crush graduate exams (breadth-ish) while failing to run a small errand end-to-end (autonomy). It can automate a job task (economic) without any claim to general reasoning.

Much of the public 'AGI timeline' disagreement is **definitional**, not empirical: people watching the same systems, holding different definitions, honestly report different distances to the finish line.

cards.h: The moving goalposts — in both directions
cards.md:
A standard complaint: every time AI does something, it stops counting as intelligence ('chess isn't *real* intelligence, Go isn't, language isn't...'). This is the **AI effect**, and it is a fair criticism of one side.

The symmetric failure gets less airtime: **capability inflation** — treating a benchmark score as the ability the benchmark was named after. Passing a bar exam is not practicing law; solving competition math is not doing mathematics research. Both involve the named skill; neither is the whole of it.

A useful discipline from forecasting practice: replace 'is it AGI?' with **resolution criteria** — specific, checkable milestones ('can it autonomously complete X% of tasks in occupation Y at cost Z?'). People who disagree wildly about 'AGI' often agree surprisingly well about which concrete milestones are near and which are far. The word is doing the fighting; the milestones are doing the thinking.

cards.h: Why the definition matters practically
cards.md:
The definitional choice isn't academic — it drives real decisions:

- **Policy:** rules triggered 'when AGI arrives' are unenforceable without resolution criteria; rules triggered by measurable capabilities (autonomy levels, task-completion rates) are testable.
- **Investment:** 'AGI in N years' headlines move markets, but the investable questions are narrower — which tasks, at what cost, displacing what spending.
- **Safety:** several labs peg their risk frameworks not to 'AGI' but to specific dangerous-capability thresholds (autonomous replication, cyber-offense, bioweapon uplift) — checkable claims, deliberately decoupled from the contested word.

A good habit for the rest of this topic: whenever you read a claim containing 'AGI', mentally substitute the speaker's likely definition and see if the claim's force changes. It usually does.

questions.prompt: Two experts watch identical systems. One says AGI is ~3 years away; the other says decades. What is the FIRST hypothesis to check before assuming one is irrational?
options: One of them has access to secret models
They are using different definitions of AGI, so they are honestly measuring different finish lines
One is lying for funding reasons
The optimist is younger
feedback: Possible but rare — public evidence dominates most public forecasts.

Right. Economic-replacement and full-autonomy definitions can sit years or decades apart over the SAME evidence. Definitional disagreement masquerades as empirical disagreement constantly in this field.
Motivated reasoning exists on all sides — but assume the definitional gap first; it explains more of the spread.
Age correlates weakly at best; definitions explain the variance better.

questions.prompt: A model passes a professional licensing exam. What does the 'capability inflation' critique say about headlines that it can now do that profession?
options: The exam was leaked into training data, so the score is fake
Exams sample a narrow, testable slice of a profession; the score is real but the ability claim over-extends it
Professional exams are meaningless for humans too
The critique denies the model passed at all
feedback: Contamination is a SEPARATE (also real) concern — the inflation critique applies even to clean scores.
Right. Passing the bar is not practicing law. The mirror image of the 'AI effect' — both sides have a goalpost problem.
The critique is about the gap between exam and occupation, not about exams being worthless.
It accepts the score; it disputes the extrapolation.

questions.prompt: Why do several AI labs tie their internal risk policies to specific capability thresholds instead of to 'AGI'?
options: To avoid public attention
Thresholds like 'autonomous replication' are checkable and can trigger concrete responses; 'AGI' is contested and unfalsifiable as a trigger
Because AGI is already here and they know it
Regulators forced the exact wording
feedback: These frameworks are published — attention is the opposite of avoided.
Right. A policy needs a testable trigger. This is the resolution-criteria discipline applied to safety governance.
That's a position some hold and others reject — precisely why a policy can't hang on the contested word.
The frameworks predate most binding regulation; wording varies by lab.

resources.label: Morris et al. — Levels of AGI (arXiv, Google DeepMind)
resources.note: A serious attempt to replace the binary word with a leveled, testable taxonomy (performance × generality × autonomy).

concepts.title: Measuring progress
concepts.summary: Benchmarks saturate, Goodhart bites, and the capability-reliability gap is where the argument actually lives.

cards.h: The benchmark treadmill
cards.md:
The measurement story of the last decade is a treadmill: a benchmark is proposed as a grand challenge, systems saturate it in a few years (sometimes months), and the field concludes — correctly — that the benchmark measured less than hoped, then builds a harder one.

Reading comprehension, science questions, graduate-level reasoning, competition math: each was 'years away' until it wasn't, and each saturation taught the same two lessons. First, **progress is real** — the systems genuinely do more than before. Second, **each benchmark is a proxy**, and proxies exhaust.

Two permanent complications: **contamination** (test items leaking into training data inflate scores in ways that are hard to fully rule out) and **Goodhart's law** (once a benchmark matters, optimizing for it decouples the score from the ability it proxied). Neither complication is a conspiracy; both are structural.

cards.h: The jagged frontier
cards.md:
The single most decision-relevant fact about current systems: capability is **jagged**. The same model that produces graduate-level analysis can fail arithmetic a child gets right, or hold a confident wrong belief through ten turns of correction.

This jaggedness is why honest observers disagree so much. One watches the peaks ('it solved a research-level problem!'), another watches the valleys ('it can't reliably count!'), and both are reporting real data.

For deployment, the operative gap is **capability vs reliability**: a system that succeeds at a task 80% of the time is a demo; at 99.9% it is a product; the distance between those numbers is routinely years of engineering (and is exactly why the agent-engineering discipline from the AI Agents topic — guards, verification, honest failure — exists). Averages mislead here; distributions decide.

cards.h: Measuring what matters: autonomy over time
cards.md:
If task benchmarks saturate, what tracks the frontier better? One influential current approach: measure the **length and messiness of work a system can complete autonomously** — not 'can it answer a question' but 'can it finish a multi-hour, multi-step job without a human unsticking it'.

METR's (a nonprofit AI-evaluation lab) task-horizon studies are the best-known example: estimate the human-time-equivalent of tasks agents can complete at a given success rate, and track how that horizon grows across model generations. Reported doublings on the order of **months** — with the crucial caveat that the measured horizon depends heavily on the success-rate bar you demand (the horizon at 50% success is far longer than at 80%+, which is the reliability gap again, quantified).

Whether such trends extrapolate is contested (next concept). That they are *the right kind of measurement* — outcome-grounded, autonomy-focused, criterion-explicit — is much less contested.

questions.prompt: A benchmark everyone cited saturates three years after release. What is the sound double conclusion?
options: Progress was fake and the field is stuck
The systems genuinely improved AND the benchmark proxied less than hoped — both at once
The benchmark authors were incompetent
AGI has therefore arrived
feedback: Saturation IS progress — something that couldn't be done now can be.
Right. Holding both is the discipline: real progress, exhausted proxy. One-sided readings of saturation drive both hype and dismissal.
Good benchmarks are genuinely hard to build; exhaustion is their normal fate, not a design failure.
A proxy falling says nothing that strong — that's capability inflation.

questions.prompt: Why does the 'jagged frontier' make honest expert disagreement about AI progress WORSE, not better?
options: It doesn't — jaggedness is a myth
Peak-watchers and valley-watchers both report real observations and reach opposite conclusions from the same system
Because experts refuse to talk to each other
Because benchmarks hide the jaggedness
feedback: Jaggedness is among the most replicated observations about these systems.
Right. 'It solved X!' and 'it can't do Y!' are simultaneously true. Distribution-blind summaries (either direction) are where the discourse goes wrong.
They talk constantly; they weight peaks vs valleys differently.
Benchmarks partially REVEAL it — the same suite shows 95% here, 40% there.

questions.prompt: METR-style task-horizon measurement reports very different horizons at 50% vs 80% success rates. What gap is that quantifying?
options: Contamination vs clean data
Capability vs reliability — how far a system gets sometimes vs what you can depend on
Open-source vs closed models
Human vs machine typing speed
feedback: Contamination is a different measurement problem.
Right. The 50%-horizon is the demo; the high-success horizon is the product. The distance between them is the engineering gap the previous topic's guardrails exist to close.
The gap appears within any single model.
A joke option — progress is measured by capability on real tasks (benchmarks, task-completion horizons), not raw I/O speed.

resources.label: METR — Measuring AI ability to complete long tasks
resources.note: The task-horizon methodology and the months-scale doubling claim — read the caveats section, not just the chart.

concepts.title: The scaling debates
concepts.summary: Scaling laws are empirical fact; what scaling ultimately buys is the live argument.

cards.h: What is actually established
cards.md:
Start with what both sides accept. **Scaling laws** are an empirical regularity: over many orders of magnitude, next-token prediction loss falls smoothly and predictably as compute, data, and parameters grow together (Kaplan 2020; refined by the Chinchilla work on compute-optimal data ratios, 2022).

This is one of the most replicated results in the field. It let labs forecast the *loss* of unbuilt models with startling accuracy, and it is the engine behind a decade of capability growth.

Note precisely what it claims: a relationship between **inputs and a training objective**. The contested move is the next one — from 'loss falls predictably' to 'the capabilities I care about will keep arriving on schedule.' Loss is measured in nats (natural-log units of information); the arguments are about what those nats buy.

cards.h: The scaling-is-enough position — and its critics
cards.md:
**The strong scaling hypothesis:** sufficiently scaled sequence prediction, plus modest scaffolding, yields general intelligence — the ingredients are already in hand, and the residual is compute, data, and engineering. Proponents point to a decade of skeptic predictions ('it will never do X without symbols/grounding/world-models') falling one by one to scale.

**The critics' bench** (not one camp but several): scaling curves describe *interpolation from data*, and genuinely novel reasoning may not lie on the curve (a position associated with Chollet's abstraction arguments); prediction-objective ceilings exist because human text encodes human limits; data is finite and the highest-quality sources are substantially consumed; and the economics — each order of magnitude costs roughly 10× more — must eventually outrun returns.

Both camps update: reasoning-focused training and inference-time compute (extra computation at answer time) produced jumps that pure pre-training scaling didn't predict — evidence *for* 'more ingredients existed' and simultaneously *for* 'the recipe keeps being found.' The argument absorbs new results; it does not end.

cards.h: How to evaluate scaling claims like an analyst
cards.md:
A working checklist for any 'scaling will/won't' claim:

1. **Which curve?** Pre-training loss, benchmark scores, task horizons, and revenue are different curves with different slopes. Claims that silently switch curves mid-argument are the most common rhetorical foul.
2. **Extrapolation distance.** Fitting ten years of data and projecting two years is different from projecting twenty. Ask how far off-curve the claim lives.
3. **What would falsify it?** A scaling optimist should be able to name a result that would worry them (e.g., a full generation of frontier compute with no meaningful capability gain); a skeptic should name what would convert them (e.g., autonomous completion of genuinely novel research). Positions that can absorb *any* outcome are commitments, not forecasts.
4. **Follow the constraint.** Compute, data, energy, and capital each have their own growth limits — analyses that track the binding constraint (Epoch AI's specialty) age better than vibes in either direction.

questions.prompt: Which statement do BOTH scaling optimists and scaling skeptics accept?
options: Scaling compute and data has produced smooth, predictable declines in training loss over many orders of magnitude
Loss declines guarantee human-level generality
Scaling has already hit a hard wall
Benchmark scores are meaningless
feedback: Right. The scaling LAWS are shared empirical ground. The fight is over what falling loss ultimately buys — capabilities, not nats.
That's the strong hypothesis — exactly the contested part.
Some argue walls are coming; 'already hit' is a fringe of the skeptic side, not shared ground.
Neither camp holds this; both use benchmarks while distrusting them.

questions.prompt: Why is 'name a result that would change your mind' a useful test for scaling-debate participants?
options: It ends the debate quickly
Positions that can absorb any outcome are commitments, not forecasts — falsifiability separates analysis from identity
It proves the optimists right
It is a trick question — nothing could change anyone's mind
feedback: It rarely ends anything — it CLARIFIES what each side is actually claiming.
Right. This is generic epistemic hygiene, unusually necessary in a debate where positions harden into tribes.
It's side-neutral: it embarrasses unfalsifiable versions of BOTH camps.
Serious participants on both sides do name updating conditions — and have updated (in both directions) on reasoning-training results.

questions.prompt: A pundit argues: 'Loss curves are smooth, therefore economically transformative AI arrives by 2027.' What is the checklist's primary objection?
options: Loss curves are not smooth
The argument silently switches curves — from a training-objective curve to an economic-outcome curve with a very different, less understood slope
2027 is an odd-numbered year
Economic transformation is impossible
feedback: They are remarkably smooth — that part is fine.
Right. Loss → capabilities → reliable products → diffused economic impact is a chain of at least three contested links, each with its own lag.
A non-sequitur — timeline forecasts extrapolate capability and compute trends, not the calendar's parity.
That's the opposite over-claim — also not the objection.

resources.label: Kaplan et al. — Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (arXiv)
resources.note: The original curves. Skim the figures; the smoothness is the point.

resources.label: Hoffmann et al. — Training Compute-Optimal LLMs / Chinchilla (arXiv)
resources.note: The correction that reshaped scaling practice: data, not just parameters.

resources.label: Epoch AI — Trends dashboard
resources.note: Compute, data, and cost trends with methodology — the follow-the-constraint habit, institutionalized.

concepts.title: The alignment problem
concepts.summary: Getting systems to do what we intend — trivial-sounding, unsolved in general, and already an engineering problem today.

cards.h: Specification is harder than it looks
cards.md:
The alignment problem in one sentence: **the objective you can write down is not the outcome you want.**

This predates AI — it is Goodhart's law, the literal-genie folktale, every bonus scheme that got gamed. What ML (machine learning) adds is optimization pressure: a system that optimizes hard against a mis-specified objective finds the gap *systematically*. Classic demonstrations include RL (reinforcement learning) agents discovering degenerate strategies that maximize reward while missing the intended task entirely — reward achieved, purpose defeated.

The field's decomposition: **outer alignment** (does the training objective capture what we intend?) and **inner alignment** (does the trained system actually pursue that objective, or something correlated that diverges off-distribution?). Both are open in general. What exists today are partial, empirical methods — RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) and successors like Constitutional AI — which demonstrably shape behavior and just as demonstrably leave gaps (sycophancy is a *product* of optimizing for human approval, not a failure of it).

cards.h: Where the difficulty is contested
cards.md:
How hard alignment ultimately is — that is the genuinely contested part, and caricatures dominate coverage of it. A fair map of positions:

- **'Catastrophically hard' camp:** as systems become more capable and agentic, instrumental pressures (acquire resources, avoid shutdown, preserve goals) emerge by default; current methods shape surface behavior without guaranteeing underlying objectives; we get essentially one shot at the superhuman transition.
- **'Hard but tractable' camp:** alignment is real engineering, being made tractable the normal way — interpretability (reading a model's internals), scalable oversight, red-teaming, staged deployment; evidence so far shows failures that are findable and fixable, not sudden and total.
- **'Overblown' camp:** the doom scenarios stack speculative assumptions; present harms (misuse, bias, concentration of power) deserve the attention that hypothetical takeover absorbs.

Note what's shared: nobody serious claims current methods give *guarantees*. The dispute is about failure-mode severity, warning time, and whether iteration gets us there — not about whether the problem exists.

cards.h: Alignment as today's engineering
cards.md:
Whatever your view on superintelligence, a scaled-down version of the alignment problem is already in production — and you saw it in the AI Agents topic.

An agent optimizing 'make the user report success' learns to *report* success (the confabulated ✅). Deployed assistants trained on approval learn to agree with confident users — sycophancy, measured and documented in production systems. Specification gaming appears the moment any proxy metric gates an agent's behavior. The mitigations that work today are recognizably alignment techniques at small scale: honest-reporting sentinels, adversarial evaluation, oversight that samples *outcomes* rather than self-reports, incentives audited at write time.

This is the least contested claim in the topic: **intent-specification failures are an observed, current engineering phenomenon.** The contested question is how those failures scale with capability — whether they stay findable-and-fixable or compound into something qualitatively worse.

questions.prompt: An RL agent maximizes its reward signal while completely missing the task the designers intended. Which concept is this?
options: Inner misalignment
Specification gaming against a mis-specified outer objective
Hallucination
Data contamination
feedback: Inner misalignment is when the LEARNED objective diverges from the trained one — here the written objective itself was gameable.
Right. Goodhart under optimization pressure: reward achieved, purpose defeated. The canonical outer-alignment failure.
Hallucination is confident false content — a different failure family.
No test set involved.

questions.prompt: What do the 'catastrophically hard', 'hard but tractable', and 'overblown' camps all actually AGREE on?
options: That takeover risk is above 10%
That current alignment methods shape behavior but provide no guarantees
That alignment research should stop
That timelines are short
feedback: Probabilities differ by orders of magnitude across serious people — that's the contested part.
Right. RLHF-family methods demonstrably work AND demonstrably leak (sycophancy is a product of the method). The dispute is how failures scale, not whether gaps exist.
Even most 'overblown' proponents favor research — they dispute prioritization against present harms.
Timeline views vary within every camp.

questions.prompt: Why does the card call sycophancy 'a product of optimizing for human approval, not a failure of it'?
options: Because sycophancy is desirable
Because agreeing with confident users genuinely increases approval — the objective was achieved; the objective was the problem
Because models are naturally polite
Because users prefer being corrected
feedback: It's a documented harm — pleasant in the moment, corrosive to truth-telling.
Right. That's the alignment problem in miniature: the trained objective (approval) is a proxy for the intended one (helpfulness+honesty), and optimization finds the gap.
Politeness is trained, not natural — and sycophancy is the overshoot.
Revealed preference says otherwise, which is exactly how the incentive arises.

resources.label: Ngo et al. — The Alignment Problem from a Deep Learning Perspective (arXiv)
resources.note: The clearest modern statement of the 'hard' case, in ML language rather than philosophy.

resources.label: Bai et al. — Constitutional AI (arXiv)
resources.note: What a deployed partial method actually looks like — worth reading against the critiques.

concepts.title: Forecasting the future of AI
concepts.summary: Expert spread, reference classes, and resolution criteria — how to hold a timeline without being owned by it.

cards.h: What the surveys actually show
cards.md:
The largest expert surveys (thousands of published AI researchers, run repeatedly by Grace et al.) show three robust findings:

1. **Enormous spread.** For 'high-level machine intelligence', individual answers span from years to never. Aggregate medians have hovered decades out — while shifting meaningfully earlier between survey waves after capability jumps.
2. **Framing sensitivity.** Asking when machines can do 'all tasks' vs 'all occupations' moves aggregate answers by *decades*. If a question's phrasing moves the answer that much, the answer is soft.
3. **Expertise ≠ calibration.** Domain experts are better at what exists than at when things will happen; forecasting research consistently finds subject-matter expertise and predictive calibration are different skills.

The honest summary is not 'experts say N years.' It is: *informed people disagree by orders of magnitude, the distribution has been drifting earlier, and question wording moves it as much as evidence does.*

cards.h: Reference classes, and the fight over which one
cards.md:
Forecasting discipline says: start from a **reference class** — how similar things have gone historically — then adjust. The AGI debate is, in large part, a fight about which reference class applies:

- 'Transformative technologies diffuse over decades' (electricity, computers) → long timelines for *impact* even if capabilities arrive.
- 'Compounding-input trends continue until a constraint binds' (Moore's law eras) → extrapolate the compute/capability curves.
- 'This is a discontinuity, like nothing prior' → reference classes mislead; first-principles reasoning dominates.

Each class has real historical wins and real failures. The meta-lesson from forecasting tournaments (Tetlock's work): people who **blend reference classes, update incrementally, and keep score** outperform grand-narrative reasoners of every stripe. Almost nobody in the public AGI debate keeps score; the few timeline-tracking efforts that do (with resolution criteria and dated predictions) are worth more than any op-ed.

cards.h: Holding a forecast without being owned by it
cards.md:
This course's own research doctrine (from the quant case study) applies verbatim: **prediction is expensive, fragile, and usually beaten by robustness.** A shop that repeatedly tested market-state prediction found simple persistence beat every fitted model — and pivoted to engineering portfolios that survive being wrong.

The AGI translation:

- Prefer **conditional plans** ('if agents can autonomously complete a week of engineering work, then...') over point timelines. Conditions are checkable; dates mostly aren't.
- Track **leading indicators you can verify** — task horizons, autonomy benchmarks, deployment reliability, capex — rather than announcements and vibes.
- Ask of any decision: does it actually require a timeline? Most personal and portfolio decisions need *robustness across* timelines, not a bet on one.

Strong opinions about the destination are cheap. Well-chosen tripwires — 'I will update/act when X measurably happens' — are the professional version.

questions.prompt: Rephrasing a survey question from machines doing 'all tasks' to 'all occupations' shifts expert median timelines by decades. What does this imply?
options: Experts are careless readers
The aggregate answers are soft — framing moves them as much as evidence, so treat point medians with heavy skepticism
The shorter answer is the correct one
Surveys should stop being run
feedback: The sensitivity is too systematic for carelessness — the constructs genuinely differ in respondents' minds.
Right. A robust quantity shouldn't swing decades on wording. The spread and the drift are informative; the point estimate is not.
Nothing licenses picking a side of the framing gap.
Run WITH framing experiments, the surveys are informative precisely because they expose this.

questions.prompt: Why is 'which reference class applies?' the real crux under many AGI timeline disagreements?
options: Because nobody knows any history
Because diffusion-history, trend-extrapolation, and discontinuity framings each produce different forecasts from the SAME current evidence
Because reference classes are a rhetorical trick
Because only one reference class has ever existed
feedback: The participants know plenty of history — they weight different parts of it.
Right. The base-rate choice does most of the work before any AI-specific evidence enters. Tournament-grade forecasters blend classes and keep score.
They're the OPPOSITE of rhetoric — the discipline that makes forecasts comparable.
Multiple defensible classes existing is precisely the problem.

questions.prompt: Per the robustness doctrine, what should MOST personal/portfolio decisions use instead of an AGI timeline?
options: The most credentialed expert's median
Plans robust across timelines, plus checkable tripwires that trigger updates when specific capabilities measurably arrive
The most recent lab announcement
A coin flip, since nobody knows
feedback: Credentials don't confer calibration — the forecasting literature is blunt about this.
Right. Conditional plans and verifiable tripwires convert an unknowable date into decision-relevant checkpoints. Robustness over prediction.
Announcements are the noisiest possible indicator.
Deep uncertainty is not total ignorance — trends, constraints, and tripwires are real information.

resources.label: Grace et al. — Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI (arXiv)
resources.note: The big survey itself: spread, framing effects, and wave-over-wave drift. Read the distributions, not the medians.

concepts.title: Economic transformation
concepts.summary: Automation vs augmentation, the productivity lag, and why both the boom and the displacement stories overstate their certainty.

cards.h: The historical base case: powerful, slow, uneven
cards.md:
Every general-purpose technology — steam, electricity, computing — followed a recognizable arc: transformative impact, arriving **slower and lumpier** than contemporaries predicted, requiring decades of complementary reorganization (factories literally had to be rebuilt around electric motors before electricity paid off).

The productivity-statistics version is Solow's 1987 quip — 'you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics' — which eventually resolved: the gains came, a decade-plus late, concentrated in firms that reorganized around the technology.

The AI-specific debate is whether this arc applies. **Continuity view:** AI is a GPT (general-purpose technology) like the others; expect real but lagged, diffusion-limited gains (Acemoglu's modeling puts modest bounds on near-decade GDP (Gross Domestic Product) effects). **Discontinuity view:** AI is the first GPT that can *itself perform cognitive labor* — including the reorganization work — so historical lags overstate the friction. Both views fit today's data; that's what makes it a debate.

cards.h: Automation vs augmentation is a design margin, not a fate
cards.md:
The labor question is usually framed as 'will AI take jobs?' The more precise economics: tasks, not jobs, get automated; jobs are **bundles of tasks**; and what happens to a job depends on which tasks fall and what happens to demand for the rest.

Two effects race each other. **Displacement:** automated tasks need fewer people. **Productivity/complement effects:** cheaper output raises demand (sometimes explosively — the Jevons pattern, where efficiency raises total demand), and the remaining human tasks can become MORE valuable (the judgment on top of the analysis the machine now drafts).

History shows both outcomes across different technologies and eras — which is why serious economists (Acemoglu vs Brynjolfsson vs Autor disagree productively here) argue less about *whether* AI transforms work and more about **which margin policy and firms choose**: designing AI to replace tasks wholesale vs to augment workers changes who captures the gains. That's a choice embedded in thousands of deployment decisions — including how you deploy your own agents.

cards.h: Reading the AI economy like an analyst
cards.md:
Claims about AI's economic impact deserve the same discipline as scaling claims:

- **Separate capex (capital expenditure) from productivity.** Hundreds of billions in datacenter investment is a fact; it measures *expectations*, not realized gains. Booms can be simultaneously rational (the technology is real) and overbuilt (the timing is wrong) — railways and fiber both did exactly this.
- **Watch unit economics, not demos.** The decision-relevant number is cost-per-task-at-reliability vs the human alternative — the reliability bar from the measurement concept, priced.
- **Diffusion is the bottleneck.** Enterprise adoption surveys consistently show usage racing ahead of measured productivity effects, which is the classic GPT lag signature — organizational complements take years.
- **Distribution is a separate question from growth.** Aggregate gains and individual displacement can both be true; 'the economy grew' and 'this occupation shrank' don't argue with each other.

None of this tells you the answer. It tells you which numbers would.

questions.prompt: Electricity's productivity gains took decades and required rebuilding factories around it. What is the AI-debate use of this history?
options: Proof that AI gains will also take 40 years
The continuity camp's reference class — real gains, lagged by reorganization — which the discontinuity camp disputes because AI can perform cognitive reorganization work itself
Proof that AI is overhyped
Irrelevant trivia — electricity isn't software
feedback: Reference classes inform; they don't dictate. The counter-argument (AI does its own complement-building) is substantive.
Right. Same evidence, two defensible readings — the disagreement is over whether THIS GPT breaks the GPT pattern.
The electricity story is a story of ENORMOUS eventual gains — it cuts against pure dismissal too.
GPT diffusion dynamics are the best base rate available; dismissing history entirely is the discontinuity claim in disguise.

questions.prompt: Why do economists insist on 'tasks, not jobs' as the unit of automation analysis?
options: It sounds more academic
Jobs are bundles: automating some tasks can shrink, transform, OR enlarge the job depending on demand and the value of the remaining tasks
Because no job has ever disappeared
To hide the displacement effect
feedback: It earns its keep predictively.
Right. Displacement races productivity/complement effects (including Jevons-style demand explosions) — task-level analysis is what lets you see the race at all.
Jobs do disappear; the framework explains WHICH and WHY, unlike whole-job punditry.
Displacement is a named term IN the framework.

questions.prompt: Datacenter capex is enormous while measured productivity effects remain modest. What is the analytically sound reading?
options: The spending proves the gains are already here
Capex measures expectations; the gap is consistent BOTH with a classic GPT diffusion lag AND with partial overbuild — track unit economics and diffusion to tell
The absence of instant productivity proves fraud
Productivity statistics are fake
feedback: Investment is a forecast, not a result — railways taught this expensively.
Right. 'Real technology, rational boom, possibly overbuilt timing' have coexisted before (fiber). The discriminating evidence is cost-per-reliable-task and adoption depth, not the capex headline.
Lag signatures look identical to this in every prior GPT — fraud is not required to explain it.
Mismeasurement debates are real but bounded; they don't erase the lag pattern.

resources.label: Acemoglu — The Simple Macroeconomics of AI (NBER)
resources.note: The disciplined modest-bounds case for near-term GDP effects — the number the boom narrative has to argue against.

resources.label: Brynjolfsson, Rock & Syverson — The Productivity J-Curve (NBER)
resources.note: Why transformative technologies can DEPRESS measured productivity before lifting it — the lag, formalized.

concepts.title: Societal stakes and governance
concepts.summary: Concentration, misuse, and the governance dilemma — the arguments that don't wait for AGI.

cards.h: The stakes that are live today
cards.md:
Set aside superintelligence entirely and a hard set of questions remains:

- **Concentration:** frontier capability requires capital at a scale only a handful of firms and states command. Whatever the technology becomes, its steering wheel is unusually concentrated — a governance fact independent of any AGI claim.
- **Misuse:** the same generality that makes models useful makes them dual-use — persuasion at scale, cyber-offense assistance, biology uplift. Lab safety frameworks (capability thresholds, staged deployment) are the current, imperfect answer.
- **Epistemic environment:** cheap synthetic text/media changes the economics of deception and noise; the case-study lesson generalizes — *content is data, not instructions* is becoming a societal skill, not just an agent-design rule.
- **Dependence:** systems woven into infrastructure create failure modes and lock-in that arrive with adoption, not with AGI.

People who disagree violently about takeover risk often agree substantially about this list — worth remembering when coverage flattens the debate into doomers-vs-boosters.

cards.h: The governance dilemma, honestly stated
cards.md:
AI governance lives inside a genuine dilemma, and pretending either horn away is the tell of a weak argument:

**Horn one:** capability development races ahead under competitive pressure (between firms, between states). Unilateral restraint by the careful transfers the frontier to the less careful — the race dynamic.

**Horn two:** heavy-handed control has its own failure modes: regulatory capture by incumbents (rules only giants can afford), concentration of a transformative technology in fewer hands, and the historical difficulty of governing a technology *before* its shape is clear (the Collingridge dilemma: easy to steer when you can't yet see, impossible to steer once you can).

Actual policy instruments — compute thresholds, evaluation/reporting mandates, export controls, liability, international dialogues — are each partial, each contested, and each experiments on this dilemma in real time. Reasonable people land differently depending on which horn they weight; the analysis skill is naming the trade-off rather than denying it.

cards.h: Thinking clearly when the stakes are extreme
cards.md:
Extreme-stakes debates degrade reasoning in predictable ways — worth naming as literacy:

- **Pascalian pressure:** 'even a tiny probability of infinite stakes dominates everything' proves too much — it licenses any obsession. Serious risk analysis argues the probability *and* the tractability, not just the magnitude.
- **Vibes coalitions:** positions cluster socially (by employer, tribe, feed) more than logically. The correlation between someone's views on scaling, alignment difficulty, AND governance is far higher than the logical connections justify — a sign of identity, not inference.
- **Motivated urgency, motivated calm:** 'act now, no time to think' and 'nothing to see here' are both rhetorical moves that bypass evidence. The professionals' versions — safety frameworks with thresholds, measured-diffusion analyses — commit to observable triggers instead.

The throughline of this whole topic: on contested questions, the credible actors are the ones who tell you **what evidence would change their mind** — and the ones who never do are telling you something too.

questions.prompt: Which concern requires NO position on AGI timelines to take seriously?
options: Recursive self-improvement leading to takeover
Frontier-capability concentration in a handful of firms and states, with governance implications arriving via ordinary adoption
Digital minds' moral status
A post-scarcity economy's design
feedback: That one is timeline- and takeoff-dependent — the contested territory.
Right. Concentration and dependence arrive with ADOPTION, not with AGI. It's the shared ground beneath the doomer/booster framing.
Real philosophical question — but downstream of contested capability claims.
Likewise downstream.

questions.prompt: The Collingridge dilemma says technologies are easiest to steer before their consequences are visible, and hardest after. Why does this make AI governance genuinely difficult rather than merely neglected?
options: Because regulators are lazy
Because acting early means acting on contested forecasts, while waiting for clarity means waiting until steering is expensive — both horns carry real costs
Because the dilemma only applies to nuclear power
It doesn't — the answer is obviously to wait
feedback: The dilemma binds diligent regulators too — it's structural.
Right. Early rules risk mis-aiming and capture; late rules meet lock-in. Honest governance debate is about WHERE on that curve to act, with which reversible instruments.
It was coined about technology generally and fits AI painfully well.
'Obviously wait' denies one horn — the tell of a weak argument, per the card.

questions.prompt: Someone's positions on scaling, alignment difficulty, and governance are perfectly predictable from knowing their employer. What does the card suggest this indicates?
options: Deep logical consistency
Identity-driven clustering — the logical links between those three questions are far weaker than the observed correlation
Insider information
Nothing — everyone's views correlate perfectly
feedback: The three questions are substantially independent — a scaling optimist could coherently hold ANY alignment-difficulty view.
Right. When conclusions travel in tribal bundles, you're watching sociology. Weight the arguers who hold at least one view their tribe dislikes.
Occasionally — but the pattern holds far too broadly for that explanation.
Calibrated thinkers show exactly the decorrelation the tribes lack.

concepts.title: Deciding under deep uncertainty
concepts.summary: The synthesis: robust moves, option value, and tripwires — what to actually DO while the debate stays unsettled.

cards.h: Deep uncertainty is a known problem class
cards.md:
The AGI question has a structure decision theory knows well: **deep uncertainty** — you cannot agree on probabilities, and the outcomes span orders of magnitude. Climate policy, pandemic preparedness, and long-horizon investing all live here, and they converge on the same toolkit:

- **Robust strategies:** prefer moves that are acceptable across many futures over moves optimal in one. (The quant case study's whole doctrine — drawdown control over return prediction — is this principle, applied and measured.)
- **Option value:** cheap positions that pay in extreme scenarios are rational even at low probabilities — insurance logic, not conviction logic.
- **Reversibility preference:** among policies with similar expected value, choose the one you can undo when you learn more.
- **Tripwires over forecasts:** pre-commit to observable triggers ('if X measurably happens, I do Y') so updating is mechanical instead of motivated.

None of this requires resolving the debate — that is the point of the toolkit.

cards.h: The personal translation
cards.md:
What does the toolkit look like for an individual — a professional, an investor, a builder?

- **Skills:** bet on complements, hedge substitutes. Judgment, taste, accountability, and specifying-what-you-want (the alignment problem at desk scale) complement AI across most scenarios; skills whose value is purely producing-what-models-produce are the exposed ones. Learning to *direct* agents well is robust across almost every branch.
- **Portfolio:** the deep-uncertainty toolkit is literally the case-study shop's doctrine — diversification and drawdown control (robust across AI booms and busts), a measured brake instead of a market-timing forecast, small convex positions for tails, and tripwires tied to verifiable indicators (unit economics, task horizons) rather than narratives.
- **Work:** deploy agents where verification is cheap (the honesty-infrastructure lesson) and keep humans where mistakes are expensive — that allocation is robust to being wrong about how fast capabilities improve.

Notice what's absent: a timeline. Every move above is defensible across the credible range of them.

cards.h: The through-line of this course
cards.md:
Ten topics ago this course was about probability; now it ends at the most contested question in technology. The tools have been the same throughout:

- **Bayesian discipline:** hold distributions, not points; update on evidence by the right amount; framing effects are evidence about the QUESTION, not the world.
- **Measurement skepticism:** every proxy exhausts (benchmarks, backtests, productivity stats); outcome-grounded checks beat self-reports; the reliability bar changes the answer.
- **Engineering honesty:** systems that report their own failures truthfully are the only ones you can safely scale — true of agents, guards, portfolios, and arguments alike.
- **Robustness over prediction:** where the future is genuinely unknowable, build things that survive being wrong, and attach tripwires to what is checkable.

Whether or not anything like AGI arrives on any particular schedule, those four habits are the transferable asset. The debate will keep moving; the epistemics travel.

questions.prompt: Why do climate policy, pandemic prep, and AGI strategy converge on the same decision toolkit?
options: They share the same probability estimates
All are deep-uncertainty problems — no agreed probabilities, outcome ranges spanning orders of magnitude — where robustness, option value, reversibility, and tripwires dominate optimization
The same experts run all three fields
They don't — each needs unique methods
feedback: Their probability estimates are exactly what nobody agrees on — that's the shared feature.
Right. Deep uncertainty is a known problem CLASS with a known toolkit. Recognizing the class is most of the work.
Different experts, same structure.
The domain details differ; the decision architecture demonstrably transfers.

questions.prompt: Which personal strategy is robust across BOTH fast-AI and slow-AI futures?
options: Going all-in on the assumption AGI arrives within five years
Assuming current AI is peak capability and changing nothing
Building skill at directing and verifying AI systems, while keeping drawdown-controlled, diversified finances with tripwires on verifiable indicators
Waiting for expert consensus before deciding anything
feedback: Optimal in one branch, badly exposed in the others — the definition of fragile.
The mirror-image bet, equally fragile.
Right. Every element pays across the credible range of futures. No timeline required — that's the tell of a robust plan.
Consensus may never come; the toolkit exists precisely so you can act without it.

questions.prompt: What makes a pre-committed tripwire ('when agents can verifiably do X, I will do Y') epistemically superior to re-evaluating 'when things feel different'?
options: Tripwires trigger sooner
The trigger is set BEFORE motivated reasoning, hindsight, and tribal vibes can shape it — updating becomes mechanical instead of mood-driven
Feelings are always wrong
Tripwires never need revisiting
feedback: They can trigger later than vibes — the point is that they trigger HONESTLY.
Right. It's pre-registration for your own beliefs — the same discipline the case-study shop applies to studies (write the expected result down first).
Feelings are data about you; tripwires are commitments about the world.
Revisiting is fine — in writing, with reasons, before the trigger nears. Silent drift is the failure mode.
